claim: CCO-deficient cell patches are rare and randomly distributed within the airways.
source: These patches were rare and randomly distributed within the airways (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by Figure 1A showing distribution of patches

claim: No CCO-deficient individual cells or patches were found in the 25 year old patient despite examination of over one million cells.
source: Consistent with previous observations, no CCO-deficient individual cells, or patches of cells, were found in the 25 year old patient, despite examination of over one million cells, placing a constraint on the time taken for the chance clonal selection of a single mitochondrial mutation within an individual cell (Greaves et al., 2006).
evidence: Direct observation from experimental data with citation to previous work

claim: mtDNA mutations are random and increase with age.
source: mtDNA mutations are random and increase with age (Brierley et al., 1998; Michikawa et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: For the mutated mitochondrial CCO genotype to result in a loss of CCO expression, homoplasmy or high levels of heteroplasmy must be present.
source: For the mutated mitochondrial CCO genotype to result in a loss of CCO expression, homoplasmy or high levels of heteroplasmy must be present (Sciacco et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: CCO-deficient clonal patches contain keratin 5 positive basal cells.
source: (E) CCO-deficient clonal patches contain keratin 5 positive basal cells (blue; arrowhead)
evidence: Shown in Figure 1E with immunofluorescence staining

claim: CCO-deficient clonal patches contain acetylated tubulin positive ciliated cells.
source: (F) acetylated tubulin positive ciliated cells (blue; arrowhead)
evidence: Shown in Figure 1F with immunofluorescence staining

claim: CCO-deficient clonal patches contain Mucin 5AC positive goblet cells.
source: (G) Mucin 5AC positive goblet cells (blue: arrowhead)
evidence: Shown in Figure 1G with immunofluorescence staining

claim: There was no difference in lineage-specific differentiation between the CCO-deficient patches and the CCO-active lung epithelial cells.
source: (H) There was no difference in lineage-specific differentiation between the CCO-deficient patches and the CCO-active lung epithelial cells. Cell percentages were calculated after counting all cells from 11 CCO-deficient patches and 11 CCO-active patches (basal cells–34.7 ± 2.1 vs 36.7 ± 6.5; ciliated cells–45.7 ± 1.7 vs 44 ± 7.2, Goblet cells–19.6 ± 2.1 vs 19.3 ± 13.5 [mean ± SD]).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of cell type percentages from experimental data

claim: Cells within individual CCO-deficient patches are clonally derived.
source: Cells within individual CCO-deficient patches were demonstrated as clonally derived by single cell laser microdissection and subsequent mitochondrial genome sequencing (Figure 2A–F).
evidence: Demonstrated through mitochondrial genome sequencing of individual cells

claim: A 9850 T>C homoplasmic mutation was found in all CCO-deficient lung epithelial cells within one patch while all CCO-normal cells maintained their wild-type genotype.
source: Within the patch shown in Figure 2A, a 9850 T>C homoplasmic mutation was found in all CCO-deficient lung epithelial cells (Figure 2B) while all CCO-normal cells maintained their wild-type genotype (Figure 2C).
evidence: Direct sequencing data from specific patch

claim: The 9850 T>C mtDNA mutation results in a Leu215Pro amino acid substitution in cytochrome c oxidase protein predicting the identified CCO deficiency.
source: This 9850 T>C mtDNA mutation is present in the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase III gene, and results in a Leu215Pro amino acid substitution in cytochrome c oxidase protein predicting the identified CCO deficiency.
evidence: Inference from genetic sequence data about protein structure and function

claim: Seven CCO-deficient patches from three patients were genetically analysed and confirmed that each patch was clonally distinct.
source: In total, seven CCO-deficient patches of varying size from three patients were genetically analysed and confirmed that each patch was clonally distinct, as evidenced by patch-unique mtDNA mutations (Table 2).
evidence: Genetic sequencing data from multiple patches showing unique mutations

claim: There was no significant difference in the proliferation index between CCO-positive epithelium and CCO-negative patches.
source: There was no significant difference in the proliferation index (as measured by Ki67) between CCO-positive epithelium and CCO-negative patches (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Ki67 immunofluorescence measurements comparing CCO-positive and CCO-negative patches

claim: Only ciliated and basal cells were always present in CCO-deficient patches with more than five cells.
source: Significantly, on examining the cell types within CCO-deficient patches, only ciliated and basal cells were always present in CCO-deficient patches with more than five cells, consistent with murine data identifying basal cells as the most likely host of multipotent progenitors of the upper airway (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Cell type analysis of patches combined with comparison to murine data

claim: The majority of clones with five cells or less contain one or more basal cells.
source: While the majority of clones with five cells or less contain one or more basal cells (Figure 3E), a few small clones lack basal cells altogether suggesting basal progenitors are able to undergo terminal division leading to clone loss (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Observation from cell type analysis of small clones

claim: A few small clones lack basal cells altogether suggesting basal progenitors are able to undergo terminal division leading to clone loss.
source: While the majority of clones with five cells or less contain one or more basal cells (Figure 3E), a few small clones lack basal cells altogether suggesting basal progenitors are able to undergo terminal division leading to clone loss (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Inference from observation of clones lacking basal cells

claim: A total of 844 CCO-deficient patches were identified among 12.7 million cells studied in seven patients.
source: In total we identified 844 CCO-deficient patches among the 12.7 million cells studied in the seven patients.
evidence: Direct count from experimental observations

claim: The number of surviving clones does not increase substantially between 39 to 79 year old patients despite ongoing marking of cells through sporadic mutation.
source: However, despite the ongoing marking of cells through sporadic mutation, the number of surviving clones does not increase substantially between 39 to 79 year old patients (Figure 4A).
evidence: Clone density measurements across different patient ages

claim: The observation that clone number does not increase substantially with age provides evidence of clone loss through differentiation.
source: As well as providing further evidence of clone loss through differentiation, this result suggests that the frequency of loss and replacement may be high.
evidence: Inference from the observation of stable clone density over time

claim: The frequency of progenitor cell loss and replacement may be high.
source: As well as providing further evidence of clone loss through differentiation, this result suggests that the frequency of loss and replacement may be high.
evidence: Inference from clone density data

claim: With clonal densities of around 100/cm2, the typical separation between clones is around 100 cell diameters.
source: With clonal densities of around 100/cm2 (Figure 4A), we estimate a typical separation between clones to be around 100 cell diameters.
evidence: Calculation based on measured clone density

claim: Errors due to clone merger events are likely to play only a minor role.
source: With typical clone sizes of around 100 cells or less, this suggests that errors due to clone merger events are likely to play only a minor role.
evidence: Inference from clone size and separation measurements

claim: There is a broad distribution of clone sizes with clones as large as 30–40 cells coexisting with clones with only one or two cells.
source: From these studies, we find a broad distribution of clone sizes with clones as large as 30–40 cells coexisting with clones with only one or two cells.
evidence: Direct observation from clone size distribution data

claim: The clones show a small drift to larger sizes with increasing age, but the distributions remain broad.
source: While the clones show a small drift to larger sizes with increasing age, the distributions remain broad.
evidence: Observation from clone size distribution data across different ages

claim: Maintenance of lung epithelium involves the steady turnover of a single, multipotent, functionally equivalent (equipotent), tissue-maintaining population.
source: To develop our model, let us suppose that maintenance of lung epithelium involves the steady turnover of a single, multipotent, functionally equivalent (i.e., equipotent), tissue-maintaining population, a necessary condition of long-term tissue homeostasis.
evidence: Model assumption based on theoretical considerations of homeostasis

claim: Following division of proliferative cells, the daughters can adopt one of three possible fate outcomes: two progenitor cells, two cells that have committed to a differentiation pathway, or one progenitor and one differentiating cell.
source: Following division of these proliferative cells, the daughters can adopt one of three possible fate outcomes—two progenitor cells, two cells that have commited to a differentiation pathway (either directly or through a series of terminal divisions), or one progenitor and one differentiating cell (Figure 5A).
evidence: Model framework describing possible cell fate outcomes

claim: Symmetric divisions leading to progenitor cell duplication must be perfectly balanced by those leading to differentiation and loss to ensure long-term homeostasis.
source: To ensure long-term homeostasis, symmetric divisions leading to progenitor cell duplication must be perfectly balanced by those leading to differentiation and loss.
evidence: Theoretical requirement for tissue homeostasis

claim: Clones are predicted to follow a process of 'neutral drift' in which the chance expansion of some clones through proliferation is compensated by the contraction and extinction of others through differentiation and subsequent loss.
source: In this paradigm, clones are predicted to follow a process of 'neutral drift' in which the chance expansion of some clones through proliferation is compensated by the contraction and extinction of others through differentiation and subsequent loss (Figure 5B).
evidence: Model prediction based on balanced stochastic fate

claim: The model prediction shows excellent agreement with experimental data for all six patients (smokers and non-smokers) with CCO-deficient clones.
source: From a fit of the model prediction, Equation 1, to the raw experimental data (Figure 4B,C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), we find excellent agreement (Figure 6A,B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) for all six patients (smokers and non-smokers) with CCO-deficient clones, with the inferred values of average clone size N(t), shown in Figure 6C.
evidence: Comparison of model predictions with experimental data

claim: The multipotent progenitor cells that line the lung epithelium of the upper airways form a single, equipotent population that maintain tissue through a process of population asymmetry.
source: From the fit of the experimental data with the predicted form of the distribution, we conclude that the multipotent progenitor cells that line the lung epithelium of the upper airways form a single, equipotent population that maintain tissue through a process of population asymmetry.
evidence: Conclusion from fitting model to experimental data

claim: The chance loss of progenitors through differentiation is perfectly compensated by duplication of neighbouring progenitors leading to a neutral drift in the size of surviving clones.
source: In the course of turnover, the chance loss of progenitors through differentiation is perfectly compensated by duplication of neighbouring progenitors leading to a neutral drift in the size of surviving clones and a continual depletion in clonal diversity of tissue (Figure 5A).
evidence: Conclusion from model fitting to experimental data

claim: The values of N(t) inferred from quantitative analysis follow approximately the predicted linear time-dependence for both smokers and non-smokers.
source: In particular, for both smokers and non-smokers, the values of N(t), inferred from the quantitative analysis of the clone fate data follow approximately the predicted linear time-dependence (Figure 6C), with a rate constant of rλ/ρ = 2.7 ± 0.5/year for smokers and rλ/ρ = 1.5 ± 0.8 for non-smokers.
evidence: Analysis of clone size data across different ages

claim: The rate constant rλ/ρ is 2.7 ± 0.5/year for smokers.
source: In particular, for both smokers and non-smokers, the values of N(t), inferred from the quantitative analysis of the clone fate data follow approximately the predicted linear time-dependence (Figure 6C), with a rate constant of rλ/ρ = 2.7 ± 0.5/year for smokers and rλ/ρ = 1.5 ± 0.8 for non-smokers.
evidence: Calculated from fitting model to experimental data

claim: The rate constant rλ/ρ is 1.5 ± 0.8/year for non-smokers.
source: In particular, for both smokers and non-smokers, the values of N(t), inferred from the quantitative analysis of the clone fate data follow approximately the predicted linear time-dependence (Figure 6C), with a rate constant of rλ/ρ = 2.7 ± 0.5/year for smokers and rλ/ρ = 1.5 ± 0.8 for non-smokers.
evidence: Calculated from fitting model to experimental data

claim: CCO-deficient mutations become visible in patients at approximately 20 ± 10 years of age.
source: Moreover, from the extrapolation of N(t) to zero, we can deduce that CCO-deficient mutations become visible in patients at approximately 20 ± 10 years of age, consistent with the absence of CCO-deficient patches in the 25 year old patient.
evidence: Extrapolation from model fitting and consistent with observation in 25 year old patient

claim: The basal cell population comprises approximately one-third (ρ = 1/3) of the total lung epithelial cell population.
source: If we suppose that the basal cell population comprises the entire population of tissue-maintaining progenitor cells, from their proportion of the total lung epithelial cell population (Figure 1H) we can estimate ρ = 1/3, from which it follows that the progenitor cell loss/replacement rate is given by 2rλ = 1.8 ± 0.4/year.
evidence: Estimated from cell type composition data in Figure 1H

claim: The progenitor cell loss/replacement rate is 2rλ = 1.8 ± 0.4/year for smokers.
source: If we suppose that the basal cell population comprises the entire population of tissue-maintaining progenitor cells, from their proportion of the total lung epithelial cell population (Figure 1H) we can estimate ρ = 1/3, from which it follows that the progenitor cell loss/replacement rate is given by 2rλ = 1.8 ± 0.4/year.
evidence: Calculated from rate constant and estimated ρ value

claim: The progenitor cell loss/replacement rate for non-smokers is 2rλ = 1 ± 0.5/year.
source: Intriguingly, this compares to the inferred value for non-smokers of 2rλ = 1 ± 0.5/year, a factor of around two smaller.
evidence: Calculated from rate constant and estimated ρ value

claim: The progenitor cell loss/replacement rate in smokers is approximately a factor of two higher than in non-smokers.
source: Intriguingly, this compares to the inferred value for non-smokers of 2rλ = 1 ± 0.5/year, a factor of around two smaller.
evidence: Comparison of calculated rates between smokers and non-smokers

claim: Single cell clones are more prevalent in non-smokers than smokers, consistent with a higher rate of turnover in smokers.
source: Further support for this conclusion is found from the observation of single cell clones, which are more prevalent in non-smokers than smokers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), consistent with a higher rate of turnover in the later.
evidence: Observation from clone size distribution data with inference about turnover rate

claim: The mutation rate for smokers is R = 100 ± 10/year/cm2.
source: From the small increase in clone density in smokers from 39 to 79 years (Figure 4A), as expected from the predicted logarithmic growth dependence, using the inferred values of rλ/ρ and N(t), we find a mutation rate of R = 100 ± 10/year/cm2.
evidence: Calculated from clone density data and model parameters

claim: The mutation rate translates to the acquisition of CCO deficiency at a rate of around 10−4/cell/year for smokers.
source: With a cell density of around 106/cm2, this translates to the acquisition of CCO deficiency at a rate of around 10−4/cell/year.
evidence: Calculation from mutation rate and cell density

claim: The mutation rate for non-smokers is R = 60 ± 10/year/cm2.
source: By contrast, applied to the data for non-smokers from age 47 to 65 years, we find a mutation rate with a lower figure of R = 60 ± 10/year/cm2.
evidence: Calculated from clone density data and model parameters

claim: Maintenance of human lung epithelium involves the ongoing stochastic loss and replacement of a single, functionally equivalent, multipotent, progenitor cell population.
source: In summary, these results show that maintenance of human lung epithelium involves the ongoing stochastic loss and replacement of a single, functionally equivalent, multipotent, progenitor cell population.
evidence: Summary conclusion from all experimental and modeling results

claim: The findings are consistent with tissue-maintaining cells belonging to the pool of basal progenitors.
source: Although the clonal fate data does not unambiguously disclose the identity of this population, the findings are consistent with tissue-maintaining cells belonging to the pool of basal progenitors.
evidence: Inference from cell type composition of clones

claim: The rate of progenitor cell loss and replacement is increased in smokers.
source: Moreover, this study provides strong evidence that the rate of progenitor cell loss and replacement is increased in smokers, providing a background on which the process of field cancerisation can operate.
evidence: Conclusion from comparison of calculated rates between smokers and non-smokers

claim: Only stem cells have long enough life spans to accumulate mtDNA mutations to detectable levels of homoplasmy.
source: Since only stem cells have long enough life spans to accumulate mtDNA mutations to detectable levels of homoplasmy, a clonal population marked by a particular mtDNA mutation likely represents the progeny of a single mutated stem cell (Elson et al., 2001; Greaves et al., 2006; Fellous et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: A clonal population marked by a particular mtDNA mutation likely represents the progeny of a single mutated stem cell.
source: Since only stem cells have long enough life spans to accumulate mtDNA mutations to detectable levels of homoplasmy, a clonal population marked by a particular mtDNA mutation likely represents the progeny of a single mutated stem cell (Elson et al., 2001; Greaves et al., 2006; Fellous et al., 2009).
evidence: Inference from knowledge about mtDNA mutation accumulation with citation support

claim: Stem cell niches have been located in many human tissues using mitochondrial DNA mutation lineage tracing methodology.
source: Using this lineage tracing methodology, stem cell niches have been located in many human tissues (Elson et al., 2001; McDonald et al., 2008; Fellous et al., 2009; Gutierrez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2010; Gaisa et al., 2011b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work

claim: Whole-mount human lung imaging allowed quantitative analysis of clones to demonstrate that basal cells are the likely multipotent progenitor cells in the human upper airways.
source: Our use, for the first time, of whole-mount human lung imaging allowed us to use quantitative analysis of these clones to demonstrate both that basal cells are the likely multipotent progenitor cells in the human upper airways and that airway homeostasis is maintained in a stochastic manner.
evidence: Conclusion from quantitative analysis of clone data

claim: Airway homeostasis is maintained in a stochastic manner.
source: Our use, for the first time, of whole-mount human lung imaging allowed us to use quantitative analysis of these clones to demonstrate both that basal cells are the likely multipotent progenitor cells in the human upper airways and that airway homeostasis is maintained in a stochastic manner.
evidence: Conclusion from quantitative analysis of clone data and model fitting

claim: The demonstration that a few small clones lack basal cells is consistent with terminal differentiation of a stem cell within a said clone, which would eventually lead to its loss.
source: The demonstration that a few small clones lack basal cells is consistent with terminal differentiation of a stem cell within a said clone, which would eventually lead to its loss.
evidence: Inference from observation of clones lacking basal cells

claim: Using lineage tracing studies following injury, the presence of both unipotent and multipotent basal cells airway progenitors have been proposed in mice.
source: Curiously, using elegant lineage tracing studies following injury, the presence of both unipotent and multipotent basal cells airway progenitors have been proposed in mice (Hong et al., 2004b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous murine study

claim: The absence of large clones (>5 cells) with only basal cells suggests that the basal population of the upper airways does not include a long-lived unipotent progenitor under normal homeostatic conditions.
source: By contrast, the absence of large clones (>5 cells) with only basal cells suggests that, at least under normal homeostatic conditions, the basal population of the upper airways does not include a long-lived unipotent progenitor.
evidence: Inference from observation of clone composition

claim: In distal conducting airway epithelium of normal human lungs Clara cells make up between 11 and 22% of the epithelial population and 9% of the overall proliferative compartment.
source: In our whole mount imaging of large bronchi Clara cells are virtually absent, as found by others (Boers et al., 1998), but in distal conducting airway epithelium of normal human lungs Clara cells make up between 11 and 22% of the epithelial population and 9% of the overall proliferative compartment (Boers et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: In whole mount imaging of large bronchi Clara cells are virtually absent.
source: In our whole mount imaging of large bronchi Clara cells are virtually absent, as found by others (Boers et al., 1998), but in distal conducting airway epithelium of normal human lungs Clara cells make up between 11 and 22% of the epithelial population and 9% of the overall proliferative compartment (Boers et al., 1999).
evidence: Direct observation from imaging data with citation support

claim: A process in which progenitor cell loss was compensated by duplication of neighbouring progenitors through a coordinated process would lead to the same long-term exponential clone size distribution in two-dimensional geometry.
source: However, previous studies have shown that, in the two-dimensional geometry pertinent to the lung epithelium, a process in which progenitor cell loss was compensated by duplication of neighbouring progenitors through a coordinated process would lead to the same long-term exponential clone size distribution considered here, while the average clone size would acquire a small additional logarithmic dependence on time, which would not be resolved by the current data (Klein et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous theoretical work

claim: The question of the regulatory control underlying stochastic fate specification and balance is left open.
source: As such, the question of the regulatory control underlying stochastic fate specification and balance is left open.
evidence: Explicit statement of limitation

claim: The findings do not rule out the potential for a stem/progenitor cell hierarchy, with progenitors supported by a second quiescent stem cell population.
source: In addition, these findings do not rule out the potential for a stem/progenitor cell hierarchy, with progenitors supported by a second quiescent stem cell population, as recently resolved in normal interfollicular epidermis (Mascre et al., 2012).
evidence: Explicit statement of limitation with citation to related work

claim: This study provides a benchmark to show how clones derived from the acquisition of somatic mutations can be used quantitatively to explore the pattern of homeostatic growth in other human tissues.
source: Finally, as well as its implications for the maintenance of the human airway epithelium, this study provides a benchmark to show how clones derived from the acquisition of somatic mutations can be used quantitatively to explore the pattern of homeostatic growth in other human tissues, providing a platform to investigate factors leading to dysregulation and disease.
evidence: Statement about broader implications of the methodology

claim: Human lung lobes were obtained from patients undergoing lung resection with airways taken at least 5 cm away from any tumour.
source: Human lung lobes were obtained from patients undergoing lung resection. Airways were taken at least 5 cm away from any tumour.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: The airways were histologically analysed and found normal.
source: The airways were histologically analysed and found normal.
evidence: Description of experimental validation

claim: A total number of 12.7 million cells included in seven different airways were analysed using the 100X objective of the Olympus epi-fluorescence microscope.
source: A total number of 12.7 million cells included in seven different airways were analysed using the 100X objective of the Olympus epi-fluorescence microscope.
evidence: Description of experimental scale and methods

claim: Among 12.7 million cells, 20,002 CCO-deficient cells included in 844 CCO-deficient patches were identified.
source: Among them 20,002 CCO-deficient cells included in 844 CCO-deficient patches were identified.
evidence: Direct count from experimental observations

claim: The samples mathematically analysed using the whole mount technique were from the third generation bronchi.
source: The samples mathematically analysed using the whole mount technique were from the third generation bronchi.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: The distal end of the samples were blocked and shown to be normal to regular histology assessment.
source: Importantly the distal end of the samples were blocked and shown to be normal to regular histology assessment.
evidence: Description of experimental validation

claim: CCO gene mutations occur spontaneously in all cells in a stochastic manner.
source: CCO gene mutations occur spontaneously in all cells in a stochastic manner, do not significantly affect cellular function, and are unrelated to cellular toxicant exposure (Elson et al., 2001; Taylor et al., 2001; Carew and Huang, 2002; Taylor et al., 2003; Taylor and Turnbull, 2005; Greaves et al., 2006; McDonald et al., 2008; Fellous et al., 2009; Gutierrez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2010; Gaisa et al., 2011a; Nicholson et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work

claim: CCO gene mutations do not significantly affect cellular function.
source: CCO gene mutations occur spontaneously in all cells in a stochastic manner, do not significantly affect cellular function, and are unrelated to cellular toxicant exposure (Elson et al., 2001; Taylor et al., 2001; Carew and Huang, 2002; Taylor et al., 2003; Taylor and Turnbull, 2005; Greaves et al., 2006; McDonald et al., 2008; Fellous et al., 2009; Gutierrez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2010; Gaisa et al., 2011a; Nicholson et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work

claim: CCO gene mutations are unrelated to cellular toxicant exposure.
source: CCO gene mutations occur spontaneously in all cells in a stochastic manner, do not significantly affect cellular function, and are unrelated to cellular toxicant exposure (Elson et al., 2001; Taylor et al., 2001; Carew and Huang, 2002; Taylor et al., 2003; Taylor and Turnbull, 2005; Greaves et al., 2006; McDonald et al., 2008; Fellous et al., 2009; Gutierrez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2010; Gaisa et al., 2011a; Nicholson et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work

claim: The division and accumulation of CCO-deficient cells leads to the formation of clonal patches of CCO-deficient cells within tissues, including the normal airway.
source: Thus, the division and accumulation of CCO-deficient cells leads to the formation of clonal patches of CCO-deficient cells within tissues, including the normal airway, and their examination provides a unique, histologically traceable record of airway progenitor cell fate.
evidence: Inference from knowledge about CCO mutation accumulation

claim: The examination of CCO-deficient patches provides a unique, histologically traceable record of airway progenitor cell fate.
source: Thus, the division and accumulation of CCO-deficient cells leads to the formation of clonal patches of CCO-deficient cells within tissues, including the normal airway, and their examination provides a unique, histologically traceable record of airway progenitor cell fate.
evidence: Inference from the properties of CCO mutations

claim: In both humans and mice, airways are composed of basal, ciliated, secretory, and chemosensory cell populations.
source: In both humans and mice, airways are composed of basal, ciliated, secretory, and chemosensory cell populations.
evidence: Established knowledge about airway cell composition

claim: Airway cells collectively produce antimicrobial proteins, eliminate bacteria and toxic compounds via the mucociliary escalator, warm inspired air, and act as physical barriers to exogenous particulate matter.
source: Collectively, these cells produce antimicrobial proteins, eliminate bacteria and toxic compounds via the mucociliary escalator, warm inspired air, and act as physical barriers to exogenous particulate matter (Knight and Holgate, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Previous studies of human tissue have demonstrated that basal cells can exhibit multipotent growth and differentiation properties when grown in vitro under specific conditions.
source: Previous studies of human tissue have demonstrated that basal cells can exhibit multipotent growth and differentiation properties when grown in vitro under specific conditions, while in vivo murine studies demonstrate that basal cells of the major airways function as common multipotent progenitors (Rock et al., 2009, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: In vivo murine studies demonstrate that basal cells of the major airways function as common multipotent progenitors.
source: Previous studies of human tissue have demonstrated that basal cells can exhibit multipotent growth and differentiation properties when grown in vitro under specific conditions, while in vivo murine studies demonstrate that basal cells of the major airways function as common multipotent progenitors (Rock et al., 2009, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Using lineage tracing methods involving chimeric tissue analysis and genetic cell labelling, murine airways appear to be maintained in homeostatic state by abundant progenitor cells located throughout airways.
source: Using lineage tracing methods, involving chimeric tissue analysis (Giangreco et al., 2009) and genetic cell labelling (Rawlins et al., 2009), murine airways appear to be maintained in homeostatic state by abundant progenitor cells located throughout airways.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: The range and identity of the stem cell compartment, and the frequency of stem cell loss and replacement in murine airways, has not been quantified.
source: However, the range and identity of the stem cell compartment, and the frequency of stem cell loss and replacement, has not been quantified.
evidence: Statement about gap in previous research

claim: The relevance of murine airway maintenance studies for the maintenance of human airways remains unexplored.
source: Moreover, the relevance of these studies for the maintenance of human airways remains unexplored.
evidence: Statement about gap in previous research

claim: The continuous accumulation of somatic mutations that occur in the mitochondrial genome provides a clonal record from which the self-renewal properties of the human airway stem cell population can be inferred.
source: In this study, we show that the continuous accumulation of somatic mutations that occur in the mitochondrial genome provides a clonal record from which the self-renewal properties of the human airway stem cell population can be inferred.
evidence: Main conclusion of the study

claim: The characterisation of normal tissue maintenance provides a quantitative platform from which factors promoting the dysregulation of cells leading to the development of disease can be studied.
source: Moreover, we show that the characterisation of normal tissue maintenance provides a quantitative platform from which we can study factors promoting the dysregulation of cells leading to the development of disease.
evidence: Statement about broader implications of the study

claim: The process of clonal consolidation is accelerated in the airways of smokers.
source: Further, we show that this process is accelerated in the airways of smokers, leading to intensified clonal consolidation and providing a background for tumorigenesis.
evidence: Conclusion from comparison of smoker and non-smoker data

claim: Accelerated clonal consolidation in smokers provides a background for tumorigenesis.
source: Further, we show that this process is accelerated in the airways of smokers, leading to intensified clonal consolidation and providing a background for tumorigenesis.
evidence: Inference from observed accelerated clonal dynamics in smokers

claim: The human upper airway epithelium is maintained by an equipotent basal progenitor cell population.
source: By developing a novel quantitative approach for the analysis of somatic mitochondrial mutations that are accumulated over time, we demonstrate that the human upper airway epithelium is maintained by an equipotent basal progenitor cell population, in which the chance loss of cells due to lineage commitment is perfectly compensated by the duplication of neighbours, leading to "neutral drift" of the clone population.
evidence: Main conclusion from quantitative analysis of clone data

claim: In the human upper airway epithelium, the chance loss of cells due to lineage commitment is perfectly compensated by the duplication of neighbours, leading to "neutral drift" of the clone population.
source: By developing a novel quantitative approach for the analysis of somatic mitochondrial mutations that are accumulated over time, we demonstrate that the human upper airway epithelium is maintained by an equipotent basal progenitor cell population, in which the chance loss of cells due to lineage commitment is perfectly compensated by the duplication of neighbours, leading to "neutral drift" of the clone population.
evidence: Main conclusion from quantitative analysis of clone data and model fitting

claim: Lineage tracing approaches have provided new insights into the cellular mechanisms that support tissue homeostasis in mice.
source: Lineage tracing approaches have provided new insights into the cellular mechanisms that support tissue homeostasis in mice.
evidence: Statement about previous research

claim: The relevance of murine lineage tracing discoveries to human epithelial homeostasis and its alterations in disease is unknown.
source: However, the relevance of these discoveries to human epithelial homeostasis and its alterations in disease is unknown.
evidence: Statement about gap in knowledge

claim: In skin, oesophagus, gut and testis, lineage tracing methods have demonstrated that tissue maintenance involves the continuous stochastic loss and replacement of stem cells.
source: In skin (Clayton et al., 2007; Doupe et al., 2010), oesophagus (Doupe et al., 2012), gut (Lopez-Garcia et al., 2010; Snippert et al., 2010) and testis (Klein et al., 2010), such methods have demonstrated that tissue maintenance involves the continuous stochastic loss and replacement of stem cells.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work

claim: The relevance and application of murine lineage tracing approaches to human tissues is unknown.
source: However, although such approaches provide key insights into the mechanisms of stem cell maintenance in transgenic animal models, their relevance and application to human tissues is unknown.
evidence: Statement about gap in knowledge

claim: Understanding of human airway homeostasis is limited and inferred indirectly through in vitro studies of human cell culture and murine airway models.
source: To date, our understanding of human airway homeostasis is limited and inferred indirectly through in vitro studies of human cell culture and murine airway models (Hong et al., 2004a; Schoch et al., 2004; Hajj et al., 2007; Rawlins et al., 2007; Giangreco et al., 2009; Rawlins et al., 2009; Rock et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement about current state of knowledge with citations

claim: In adults, stem cells reside at the apex of proliferative hierarchies and give rise to specialist differentiated cells.
source: In adults, stem cells reside at the apex of proliferative hierarchies and, either directly, or through a sequence of terminal divisions, give rise to the specialist differentiated cells that provide the functional properties of tissue.
evidence: Established knowledge about stem cell biology

claim: To conserve stem cell number, following division, one cell must on average remain in the stem cell compartment while the other must commit to a differentiation pathway.
